slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Malware that encrypts/locks data or systems and demands payment or another concession.

course.learn: Ransomware is malware that denies access to data or systems—commonly by encryption—and demands payment. Modern ransomware operations may also steal data for double extortion.
course.why: Ransomware can affect confidentiality, integrity, and availability and can stop business operations.
course.example: Malware encrypts shared drives, deletes shadow copies, and leaves a payment demand.
course.exam: Indicators include mass file changes, encryption, ransom notes, disabled backups, and unusual outbound exfiltration. Backups help recovery but do not replace prevention and containment.

course.learn: A Trojan disguises malicious software as something legitimate or desirable. Unlike a worm, it does not rely on self-replication as its defining behavior.
course.why: Social trust can cause users to install malware voluntarily.
course.example: A “free PDF converter” installs a remote-access backdoor along with the expected program.
course.exam: Legitimate-looking program that carries malware = Trojan.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A worm is self-replicating malware that spreads between systems, often by exploiting network services or weak credentials without needing a user to copy an infected file manually.
course.why: Rapid autonomous spread can overwhelm networks and infect many hosts quickly.
course.example: A worm scans the local network for a vulnerable service and copies itself to each vulnerable host.
course.exam: Self-replicating network spread = worm. A virus typically attaches to a host file.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Bloatware is unnecessary or unwanted software preinstalled or added to a system. It may not be malicious, but it increases attack surface, resource use, and maintenance burden.
course.why: Every unnecessary application can introduce vulnerabilities or background services that must be updated.
course.example: A new laptop ships with several unused trial applications that install services and browser extensions.
course.exam: The security response is usually remove unnecessary software as part of hardening.

course.learn: A computer virus attaches to or modifies a host file or program and replicates when that infected host executes or is shared.
course.why: Viruses can damage data and spread through user actions or file transfer.
course.example: An infected executable modifies other executables when launched.
course.exam: Virus = host file/program; worm = standalone self-spreading malware.

course.learn: A keylogger records keystrokes to capture information such as passwords, messages, or financial data. It can be software or hardware based.
course.why: It can steal secrets even when the application itself uses encryption after the user types them.
course.example: Malware records a user's credentials as they type them into a banking site.

course.learn: A logic bomb is malicious code that remains dormant until a specified condition or time triggers it.
course.why: The delayed trigger can hide the attacker's intent and make attribution harder.
course.example: A disgruntled administrator plants code that deletes files if their employee account is removed.

course.learn: A rootkit is designed to maintain privileged access while hiding itself or other malicious activity from normal system tools.
course.why: Stealth and deep privilege can make rootkits difficult to detect and remove.
course.example: A kernel-level rootkit hides malicious processes and files from standard operating-system utilities.
